title: Hypercalcaemia
subject: Medicine
summary: Hypercalcaemia is an excess of serum calcium that can arise from over‑production of PTH, malignancy, granulomatous disease, vitamin D toxicity or drugs. Clinical clues, basic investigations and first‑line management are key in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Serum ionised calcium >2.60 mmol/L (≈10.2 mg/dL) or total calcium >2.55 mmol/L (≈10.2 mg/dL) after correcting for albumin. Diagnosis requires a repeat test and exclusion of pseudohypercalcaemia.
b: Check albumin, ionised calcium if available

t.b: Is calcium above 10.2 mg/dL? A high result suggests hypercalcaemia; normalised by albumin correction.
Is ionised calcium >2.60 mmol/L? Confirms true hypercalcaemia, especially when total calcium is borderline.
Is PTH >65 pg/mL? Elevated PTH indicates primary hyperparathyroidism; low PTH points to PTH‑independent causes.
Is PTHrP >1 ng/mL? Positive in malignancy‑related hypercalcaemia.
Is 25‑OH >75 nmol/L? High levels suggest vitamin D intoxication.
Is creatinine >1.5 mg/dL? Renal impairment worsens hypercalcaemia.
Is calcium >15 mg/dL? Severe; needs IV fluids and possible bisphosphonate.

sections.p: In East Africa the commonest are infections, malignancy and herbal remedies.
b: Malignancy: squamous cell carcinoma of cervix, lung, breast; lymphoma
Drugs: thiazides, lithium, antacids with calcium
Herbal remedies: some traditional preparations contain calcium or vitamin D

t.b: Does the patient have chronic cough, weight loss or night sweats? TB can cause hypercalcaemia via activated macrophages.
Is there unexplained weight loss, night sweats or lymphadenopathy? Lymphoma may secrete PTHrP.
Has the patient taken traditional medicines? Some contain high calcium or vitamin D.

sections.p: Classic features are non‑specific but often remembered as "bones, stones, groans, psychiatric overtones".

t.b: Does the patient drink more than usual? Indicates nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Is pain localized to weight‑bearing joints? Suggests bone resorption.

sections.p: Prioritise tests that are available and give actionable information.

t.b: Confirm hypercalcaemia and assess severity.
Correct total calcium for hypoalbuminaemia.
Differentiate primary hyperparathyroidism from other causes.
Identify malignancy‑related hypercalcaemia.
Rule out vitamin D intoxication.
Assess renal function; high creatinine worsens hypercalcaemia.
Look for lung masses, TB cavities or hilar lymphadenopathy.
Detect adrenal or pancreatic lesions, gallstones.
High ratio (>0.2) suggests hypercalciuria; low ratio (<0.1) suggests low bone resorption.

sections.p: Urgent care is needed if life‑threatening complications develop.

t.b: Does the patient have prolonged QT? Hypercalcaemia shortens QT; a normal or shortened QT may be misleading.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then control calcium levels.
b: Stop offending drugs or herbal remedies
Hydrate with normal saline 1–2 L/24 h
Loop diuretics after rehydration to increase calciuresis
Bisphosphonates (e.g., pamidronate) if severe or refractory
Calcitonin for rapid but short‑term reduction
Dialysis if renal failure or refractory hypercalcaemia

t.b: Is the patient euvolemic? Start IV saline to restore volume and promote calciuresis.
After hydration, give furosemide to increase urinary calcium excretion.
Is calcium >15 mg/dL or symptomatic? Use bisphosphonate; avoid in severe renal impairment.
If rapid reduction needed, give calcitonin; avoid in pregnancy.

sections.p: Monitor calcium, renal function and treat underlying disease.
b: Check renal function weekly until stable
Educate patient on avoiding excess calcium or vitamin D
Screen for malignancy if PTHrP positive
Manage TB or other infections promptly

t.b: Is calcium returning to normal? If not, reassess cause.
Is creatinine improving? Persistent rise may need dialysis.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of hypercalcaemia in East Africa?
faq.a: Tuberculosis and other granulomatous infections are frequent, followed by squamous cell carcinomas of cervix, lung or breast.
Yes, dehydration concentrates serum calcium and reduces renal clearance, so early hydration is essential.

faq.q: Why is bisphosphonate preferred over steroids?
faq.a: Bisphosphonates inhibit bone resorption directly and are effective in malignancy‑related hypercalcaemia; steroids are mainly for vitamin D intoxication or granulomatous disease.

exam: What is the first investigation you would order in a patient with suspected hypercalcaemia? — Serum calcium (total and ionised) and albumin to confirm and quantify the excess.

A patient with hypercalcaemia and a history of TB presents with polyuria and confusion. What is the most likely mechanism? — Activated macrophages in TB produce 1,25‑OH2D, increasing intestinal calcium absorption.
You have a patient with hypercalcaemia and a normal PTH. Which test next? — PTHrP to assess for malignancy‑related hypercalcaemia.
A 45‑year‑old woman with hypercalcaemia is found to have a parathyroid adenoma on ultrasound. What is the definitive treatment? — Surgical removal of the adenoma.

During ward rounds you notice a patient with hypercalcaemia and a normal ECG. Why might the ECG be misleading? — Hypercalcaemia shortens QT; a normal QT may still be present, so clinical assessment is essential.
A patient with hypercalcaemia is started on furosemide but develops worsening renal function. What should you do? — Stop the diuretic, reassess hydration status and consider bisphosphonate therapy.
A child presents with hypercalcaemia and a history of taking herbal remedies. What is the most likely cause? — Herbal preparations containing excess calcium or vitamin D leading to hypercalcaemia.
